findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "authentication", "authorization").
findings.evidence: Definition: IAM is the global AWS service that decides who (authentication) can do what on which resource (authorization); principals are users, roles and the root account
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: Access Analyzer and last accessed data are named as the answer to 'what permissions does a role really use' but never explained.
findings.evidence: 'Real permissions used? Access Analyzer, last accessed data'
findings.fix: Add one line saying last accessed data shows which services and actions an identity actually called, and Access Analyzer can generate a least-privilege policy from CloudTrail activity. Use that to trim unused permissions.

findings.summary: One bullet holds two ideas: the Deny conditions and the override rule.
findings.evidence: "Deny on aws:SourceIp or MFA false blocks access even if another policy allows it"
findings.fix: Split it into two bullets: "Deny can use conditions such as aws:SourceIp or MFA false" and "A matching Deny blocks access even if another policy allows it".

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "definition", "security").
findings.evidence: Definition: MFA adds a second factor (virtual TOTP app, FIDO2 security key or hardware token) on top of the password; the root account is the all-powerful email-based identity created with the account
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "automatically", "credentials").
findings.evidence: Comparison: access keys are long-lived (AKIA...) and leak through code and git; role credentials are temporary (ASIA... plus session token) and expire automatically, so prefer roles for EC2, Lambda and CI
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "applications", "credentials").
findings.evidence: Interview Point: Why should the root account have no access keys? When do you still need an access key? How do you enforce MFA with a policy? How do applications on EC2 get credentials without keys?
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The outline's interview points for this section are missing: why root gets no keys, when an access key is still needed, and how EC2 apps get credentials without keys.
findings.evidence: Page 3 has sections 1-4 plus a 'Keys hygiene' note and no interview block. The only hint is the table row 'Use for | local CLI only'.
findings.fix: Add an 'Interview Point' block. Cover: root keys give full-account power and cannot be scoped; keys are still needed for local CLI or external systems that cannot assume a role; EC2 apps get credentials from an instance profile role via STS.

findings.summary: The key-rotation rule sits under the "Example: Enforce MFA" section after the code, so it is unrelated to that section and easy to miss.
findings.evidence: "4. Example: Enforce MFA ... Keys hygiene Rotate or delete any access key unused for 90 days."
findings.fix: Move the rule into section 3 "Keys vs Roles" or into its own numbered section.

findings.summary: The Root-only bullet packs several separate tasks into one line.
findings.evidence: "Root-only: change root email or password, close account, restore locked-out IAM admin"
findings.fix: Make it a short list with one task per bullet.

findings.summary: The heading "Policy Types" is reused for a different classification than page 2 (managed vs inline instead of identity vs resource-based), which can confuse a learner skimming for the term.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "2. Policy types ... Identity-based | Resource-based | Permission boundary | SCP" vs page 4: "2. Policy Types ... AWS managed | Customer managed | Inline"
findings.fix: Rename page 4's section to "Managed vs Inline Policies" and page 2's to "Policy Types by Scope".

findings.summary: The cheat sheet says everyone else should use roles or IAM Identity Center, but page 3 says daily work uses an IAM user or IAM Identity Center.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "Daily work: IAM user or IAM Identity Center" vs page 5: "Everyone else: roles or IAM Identity Center"
findings.fix: Use the same wording on both pages, for example "Daily work: IAM Identity Center or roles; IAM users only when needed".

findings.summary: The quiz answer depends on the service principal ec2.amazonaws.com, which the chapter never teaches. Trust policy is also used on pages 1 and 4 before it is defined.
findings.evidence: 'The trust policy must name ec2.amazonaws.com as Principal.' Page 1 only says 'Principals named in its trust policy', and page 4 says 'Role needs a trust policy and a permissions policy'.
findings.fix: On page 1 or 4, define a trust policy as the resource-based policy on a role that names who may assume it. Show a short example with Principal {"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"} and Action sts:AssumeRole.
